summary.oneLiner: Aro Granite Industries is India's leading exporter of processed granite, running export-oriented granite and engineered-quartz processing plants at Hosur and Jaipur and supplying more than fifty countries.
summary.business: Founded in 1988, the Company processes carefully selected raw granite into finished slabs and tiles at its Hosur (Tamil Nadu) and Jaipur plants, and since 2020 has also manufactured engineered quartz surfaces at Hosur. Products are sold to construction, home-renovation and interior-surface customers worldwide, with the Hosur plant operating as a 100% Export Oriented Unit and the Jaipur plant as a Special Economic Zone unit. The Company states an annual production capacity of one million square metres and a range of more than one hundred granite and quartz shades.

risks.risk: Export-market concentration and dependence on US trade policy
risks.note: The United States remained the Company's largest export destination, accounting for approximately 65% of total exports, with Europe around 25%, so developments in U.S. trade policy had a direct and material bearing on performance through the year.

risks.risk: Tariff regime instability and unresolved framework
risks.note: Reciprocal tariffs on Indian exports moved from 27% in April 2025 to roughly 50% by August 2025, briefly to 18% in February 2026, then were struck down and replaced by a temporary uniform 10% Section 122 surcharge - leaving a narrower, temporary and still-unresolved tariff environment with no lasting structural advantage.

risks.risk: Competitive disadvantage against competing origins on tariff and freight
risks.note: Vietnam, a key competing source for engineered quartz, negotiated its rate down to 20% in October 2025 while India's remained at or near 50%, and ocean freight from Vietnam to the US has historically been cheaper than from India - disadvantaging Indian-origin material on both tariff and logistics cost simultaneously.

Shipments from India require 55 to 75 days to reach U.S. ports, so buyers could not determine landed cost when placing orders; many deferred procurement, postponed shipments and held lower inventory, causing slower order inflows, delayed dispatches and increased pricing pressure.

risks.risk: Polyester resin / petrochemical input cost exposure
risks.note: Polyester resin constitutes approximately 60% of the raw material cost of the Company's engineered quartz slabs; the closure of the Strait of Hormuz on 28 February 2026 tightened global petrochemical supply and upward cost pressure was already visible in the final weeks of FY26.

risks.risk: Raw material availability and mining restrictions
risks.note: Raw material availability is the foremost industry challenge, made more acute by recurring mining bans on environmental and regulatory grounds in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka, limiting access to premium raw granite, disrupting supply chains and raising production costs.
FY26 capacity utilisation was 12.14% for Hosur Tiles, 10.00% for Hosur Slabs, 23.71% for Jaipur Slabs and 20.55% for Hosur Quartz, leaving a heavy fixed-cost base spread over low volumes.

risks.risk: Domestic demand held back by approval delays and material substitution
risks.note: In Bengaluru, a key domestic market, real-estate projects faced significant delays in Occupancy Certificates, e-khata records and NOCs from fire, pollution-control and utility authorities; together with cautious developer and homeowner spending and increased competition from alternative construction materials, this weighed on demand and kept pricing competitive.

risks.risk: Regulatory and compliance burden, plus skilled-labour shortage
risks.note: The sector faces strict environmental standards and intricate approval processes that can cause project delays and higher compliance costs, while workers migrating to urban centres create a skilled-labour shortage that poses risks to timely production and quality.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Demand for construction materials remained weak in the United States and Europe, and management expects the operating landscape to remain unsettled looking to FY27 and beyond.
- The U.S. tariff framework has yet to be replaced by a durable arrangement; the 10% Section 122 surcharge in effect is temporary, leaving the competitive position against competing origins unresolved.
- Tariff unpredictability directly affects order flow: shipments from India take 55 to 75 days to reach U.S. ports, so customers could not determine landed cost when ordering, and deferred procurement, postponed shipments and held lower inventory.
- Disruption to raw material markets has intensified since the year end, with petrochemical and resin prices rising sharply through March to May 2026 - a direct cost driver given polyester resin is about 60% of engineered quartz raw material cost.
- Domestic demand pressure in Bengaluru from delays in Occupancy Certificates and related clearances, cautious spending by developers and homeowners, and increased competition from alternative construction materials; pricing remained competitive, requiring focus on operational efficiency and product mix optimisation.
- Global engineered quartz surface market valued at about US$25.5 billion in 2025, up from US$23.7 billion in 2024, growing at around 7.7% a year, with North America the largest market and Asia-Pacific the fastest growing.
- In the United States countertop market, engineered quartz accounts for close to 29% of material-based demand and is expected to grow at around 7% a year.
- Urbanisation and infrastructure development in China, India and Asia-Pacific are expected to raise granite and quartz consumption materially; Indian government smart-city and urban-infrastructure initiatives should lift domestic uptake.
- The industry's shift towards value-added, premium offerings (bespoke countertops, tiles, decorative articles) is a stated margin lever for the sector.
- Management states that with earlier investments in capacity, plant modernisation and a transition towards value-added offerings, and with agile decision-making and prudent risk management, the Company is positioned to benefit as conditions stabilise.

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Diversify raw-material sourcing away from constrained South Indian quarries - the Jaipur plant was established and sourcing begun from new mines in regions such as Rajasthan and Andhra Pradesh.
- Import raw blocks to improve utilisation of the Hosur plant and maintain a steady supply of raw materials.
- Keep the engineered quartz unit at Hosur as the answer to the shift in consumer preference from natural stone towards engineered surfaces, and continue adapting the product offering.
- Run a diversified export strategy across more than fifty countries, target unique granite shades exclusive to India, and expand domestic sales to help balance currency risk.
- Strengthen supply-chain resilience by diversifying suppliers and logistics partners and using advanced inventory management systems.
- Protect long-term competitive position through tighter control of working capital, optimised production planning, disciplined inventory management and continued cost rationalisation.
- Continue the transition towards value-added offerings, building on earlier investments in capacity and plant modernisation.
- Actively evaluate alternative sourcing arrangements and pricing measures in response to the trade-policy and resin-cost environment, monitoring both closely.

Hosur operates as a 100% Export Oriented Unit and Jaipur as a Special Economic Zone unit, and the Company states an annual production capacity of one million square metres. The manufacturing-facilities spread prints installed capacities in Sq. Mt. per annum - three figures (5,85,000; 1,80,000; 3,60,000) against the Hosur site, which houses the granite slab, granite tile and engineered quartz operations, and 1,50,000 against Jaipur - but the product labels are displaced in the supplied text, so individual product-to-capacity mapping is not readable. moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Positioned as the largest processed-granite exporter of India, with a track record since 1988 and public listing in 1995
- Two-plant footprint that deliberately diversifies raw-material risk: Jaipur draws on Rajasthan quarries to offset the closure of South Indian quarries affecting Hosur
- Fiscal/structural status of the plants - Hosur a 100% Export Oriented Unit, Jaipur a Special Economic Zone unit
- Breadth of choice: more than one hundred distinguished granite shades plus an evolving quartz range
- Export spread across more than fifty countries, which the Company cites as a buffer against single-market and currency risk
- Engineered quartz line at Hosur reduces dependence on natural quarries and opens the prospect of higher margins relative to traditional granite
- Multi-Wire granite cutting machine at Hosur expanded sourcing options by enabling processing of imported rough blocks
- Workforce of over 150 individuals as at 31 March 2026 and an internal control framework reviewed by the Audit Committee
